title: How long is each piece when a ribbon is cut into ten, then a hundred?
description: A ribbon of three point nine metres is cut into ten equal pieces, then another into a hundred, and the board divides it using the reciprocal. The shorter piece is changed to centimetres and millimetres. Keeko's doubt is that dividing moves the point to the right.
teaching_notes: One idea: dividing by ten or a hundred makes every digit worth ten or a hundred times less, so the point moves left. Watch for students who move the point to the right and get a piece longer than the ribbon.

source: {{NAME_6}} cuts a 3.9 m ribbon into 10 equal pieces, then another
video_script.why: A learner who can multiply decimals sees how to divide a decimal by ten or a hundred.
video_script.substitution: Three point nine is thirty nine tenths, so a tenth of it is thirty nine hundredths.
video_script.anchor: the ribbon of three point nine metres that {{NAME_6}} cuts into equal pieces
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko moves the point to the right when dividing by ten, so a piece becomes longer than the whole ribbon.
video_script.payoff_line: The pieces are zero point three nine metres and zero point zero three nine metres long.

final_answer.value: 0.39 m and 0.039 m; 0.039 m is 3.9 cm, which is 39 mm
final_answer.spoken: zero point three nine metres and zero point zero three nine metres, and the shorter piece is thirty nine millimetres

video_script.fraction_reading: A fraction such as 39/10 is read thirty nine over ten, or thirty nine tenths when the bottom is ten.

names.{{NAME_6}}: cuts a ribbon of three point nine metres into equal pieces

maths_rules: the slip: 3.9 x 10 = 39 m, longer than the ribbon
video_script.design: One ribbon stays on the board all video; the working band builds the division with fractions, then the unit change.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a ribbon labelled 3.9 m; cut marks fall on it

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is an example from your book about {{NAME_6}} and a ribbon.
<bookmark mark='ribbon'/>The ribbon is three point nine metres long.
<bookmark mark='cut'/>{{NAME_6}} cuts it into ten equal pieces. Another ribbon of the same length is cut into a hundred equal pieces.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How long is each piece, and how many millimetres is the shorter one?

beats.on_screen: the ribbon and the question stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 3.9 = 39/10 written under the ribbon; 1/10 written beside the word reciprocal

marks.tenths: the ribbon is read as thirty nine pieces of one tenth
marks.recip: one over ten appears beside divide by ten
marks.name: the word reciprocal is written

narration: <bookmark mark='tenths'/>Three point nine is thirty nine tenths, because it holds thirty nine pieces of one tenth.
<bookmark mark='recip'/>Dividing by ten means multiplying by one over ten.
<bookmark mark='name'/>One over ten is called the reciprocal of ten.

beats.on_screen: Given: ribbon 3.9 m; cut into 10 equal pieces; another into 100 equal pieces

marks.given: the ribbon and the two cuts are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a ribbon is three point nine metres long. It is cut into ten equal pieces, and another into a hundred.

beats.on_screen: To find: length of one piece in each case; the shorter piece in cm and mm

marks.find: the two lengths and the unit change are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the length of each piece. Then we write the shorter piece in centimetres and millimetres.

marks.s1b: the product 39/100 and 0.39 m are written

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>Step one, divide by ten using the reciprocal. Thirty nine over ten times one over ten.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>That gives thirty nine over a hundred. Each of the ten pieces is zero point three nine metres.
<bookmark mark='s2a'/>Step two, divide by a hundred with its reciprocal. Thirty nine over ten times one over a hundred.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>That gives thirty nine over a thousand. Each of the hundred pieces is zero point zero three nine metres.
<bookmark mark='s3a'/>Step three, change metres to centimetres, because one metre is a hundred centimetres.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Zero point zero three nine times a hundred is three point nine centimetres.

marks.s4b: 3.9 × 10 is written with the product left blank

narration: <bookmark mark='s4a'/>Step four, change centimetres to millimetres, because one centimetre is ten millimetres.
<bookmark mark='s4b'/>We multiply three point nine by ten.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 0.39 m and 0.039 m; 0.039 m = 3.9 cm = 39 mm
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The pieces are zero point three nine metres and zero point zero three nine metres long.
<bookmark mark='mm'/>The shorter piece is three point nine centimetres, which is thirty nine millimetres.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the ribbon
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 39 m for one piece beside the 3.9 m ribbon; the bubble is crossed out; the point slides left

marks.fix: the whole ribbon is shown shorter than 39 m
marks.right: the point slides left on the digits

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks dividing by ten moves the point to the right, so each piece is thirty nine metres.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the whole ribbon is less than four metres long. A piece cannot be longer than the ribbon it came from.
<bookmark mark='right'/>Dividing makes a number smaller, so the point moves left. It moves one place for ten and two places for a hundred.
